en: The ancient Banaue Rice Terraces in the Philippines act as a giant inclined plane, reducing the effort needed to carry farming tools up the steep mountains.
The rough, carved surface of a traditional Filipino mortar and pestle increases friction to efficiently grind hard spices and garlic into a fine paste.
During the Apollo 15 mission, astronaut David Scott proved gravity acts equally on all objects by dropping a hammer and a feather on the Moon.
Japan’s SCMaglev train uses powerful superconducting magnets to levitate the vehicle above the tracks, eliminating wheel friction and allowing speeds over 600 kilometers per hour.
The Angat Hydroelectric Power Plant in Bulacan generates electricity by using the gravitational potential energy of falling water to spin large turbines.
The Philippine forest firefly produces bioluminescent light through a chemical reaction in its abdomen to attract mates in the dark jungle canopy.
The 1883 eruption of the Krakatoa volcano produced sound waves reaching 180 decibels, making it one of the loudest sounds ever recorded in history.
The Tiwi Geothermal Power Plant in Albay harnesses thermal energy by capturing naturally heated underground steam to turn turbines and generate electricity.
Water stored behind the massive concrete wall of the San Roque Dam in Pangasinan possesses high gravitational potential energy before flowing downward.
Loggers in Bukidnon use steel axes with a sharp wedge shape to concentrate force and split thick tree trunks apart efficiently.
The sleek, streamlined body of the Philippine eagle reduces air friction, allowing the massive bird to glide smoothly through the forest canopy.
Scrap yards in Quezon City use giant electromagnets powered by electricity to temporarily attract and lift heavy pieces of discarded iron and steel.
